opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is that the bottleneck has shifted. A few years ago, the hard part was getting a model to produce something reasonable at all. Now models can write code, call tools, and run multi-step tasks, so the question becomes: how quickly can you learn what actually works, and how sure are you that it works?

With agents, the feedback loop is much longer and noisier than with a single chat response. An agent might take dozens or hundreds of steps, interact with an environment, and fail for reasons that have nothing to do with the capability you're trying to improve: a flaky tool, a broken sandbox, a poorly specified task. If your evaluation isn't accurate, you can spend weeks optimizing toward noise. You think you've made progress, but you've just overfit to some quirk of your test set, or the benchmark itself is leaking answers or rewarding shortcuts.

So accurate testing is really about protecting your judgment. In research, your most valuable resource isn't compute, it's the team's attention and the direction you choose. A bad evaluation sends everyone down the wrong path with high confidence, which is worse than having no signal at all.

Research efficiency matters for a similar reason. The space of things you could try with agents is enormous: different data recipes, reward designs, environment setups, training schedules. Nobody has a complete theory, so progress comes from running many well-designed experiments and iterating fast. If one experiment takes two weeks and you can't trust the result, you get maybe twenty meaningful iterations a year. If you can get a reliable answer in two days, you're effectively playing a completely different game.

I'd also say the two are tightly connected. Efficiency without accurate testing just means you're wrong faster. Accurate testing without efficiency means you're right too slowly to matter. The teams that move well in this era are the ones who invest seriously in infrastructure, clean environments, trustworthy evals, and fast turnaround. It's not glamorous work, but it compounds. Every improvement there makes every future experiment more valuable.

r001.rationale: It says accurate evaluation lets researchers trust results and avoid optimizing toward noise, making each research attempt’s evaluation reliable.

r002.rationale: It discusses running experiments and iterating faster, but does not say different subagents can test ideas in parallel.

r003.rationale: It does not mention subagents cross-validating one another’s results.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the simplest way to put it is that in the agent era, the bottleneck has shifted. It used to be that compute or data was the scarce resource. Now, increasingly, the scarce resource is good judgment about what to try next and whether what you tried actually worked.

Let me explain what I mean. When you train a model to answer a question, the loop is fairly tight. You have a benchmark, you run it, you get a number, you iterate. But an agent is a system that takes many steps, interacts with an environment, uses tools, recovers from mistakes. The space of things that can go wrong is enormous, and a single aggregate score hides almost everything you need to know. Two agents can score the same on a leaderboard and be completely different in how they fail. One hallucinates a file path and keeps going confidently. The other stops and asks. Those are not the same product, and if your evaluation cannot distinguish them, you are flying blind.

So accurate testing, for me, is not about getting a higher number. It is about having a signal you trust enough to make decisions on. If I change the reward design or the data mixture, I need to know within a day whether that helped on the behaviors I actually care about, not just whether a proxy moved. Otherwise you end up optimizing the proxy, and agents are very good at finding the gap between the proxy and the real goal.

Research efficiency connects directly to that. Every experiment on a large agent system is expensive, in compute, in human time to inspect trajectories, in calendar time. If your evaluation is noisy, you need more runs to see a real effect, and your whole research velocity drops. If your evaluation is sharp, you can run smaller, faster experiments and still learn something. I would honestly rather have a team that runs twenty well-measured small experiments than one that runs two giant ones and argues afterward about what the result means.

There is also a cultural dimension. In a fast-moving field, there is enormous pressure to ship and to claim. Good testing is what keeps you honest with yourself. It lets you say, this works here, it does not work there, and here is the evidence. That kind of calibration compounds over time. Teams that build it early tend to make better bets later, because they actually understand their own system.

So when I say efficiency and accurate testing are crucial, I really mean they are the same thing viewed from two sides. Accurate measurement is what makes efficient research possible, and efficient research is what lets you afford accurate measurement.

r001.rationale: The response says accurate testing provides a trusted signal for judging whether an experiment helped and that sharp evaluation enables reliable learning from experiments.

r002.rationale: It discusses running experiments efficiently but does not say subagents can test different research ideas in parallel.

r003.rationale: It does not state that subagents can cross-validate one another’s research results.

astra-6.text:
I think AI agents make research efficiency and accurate testing more important because they let us try many more ideas, much faster. But generating more experiments isn’t the same as making more progress. If our tests are misleading, we can simply move faster in the wrong direction.

With agents, you also have to evaluate an entire process, not just a final answer. Did the agent understand the task? Did it choose the right actions? Could it recognize a mistake and recover? A successful result in one run doesn’t necessarily mean the system is reliable.

So these two things reinforce each other. Efficient research lets us test hypotheses quickly, and accurate testing tells us which hypotheses are actually worth pursuing. The goal is to shorten the distance between having an idea and knowing whether it works.

r001.rationale: The response says accurate testing identifies which hypotheses are worth pursuing and warns that misleading tests can send research in the wrong direction, conveying reliable evaluation of research attempts.

r002.rationale: It says agents allow more ideas to be tried faster, but does not explain that different subagents test different ideas in parallel.

r003.rationale: The response does not state that subagents cross-validate one another’s results.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI agents make both the opportunity and the bottleneck much clearer. An agent can generate code, run experiments, and propose new approaches very quickly. But producing more experiments doesn’t necessarily mean producing more knowledge. If the experiments ask the wrong questions, or the evaluation is unreliable, we can spend much more compute without making real progress.

Research efficiency, to me, means shortening the cycle from an idea to trustworthy evidence. Can we identify the key uncertainty, design an experiment that isolates it, and learn something useful even when the result is negative?

Accurate testing is what keeps that cycle grounded. For agents, we need to evaluate more than whether the final answer looks convincing. Did the agent actually complete the task? Did it recover from errors? Does it succeed consistently across different situations, and at what cost in time and resources?

These two things reinforce each other. Reliable tests tell us where to invest our research effort, and efficient research lets us improve those tests as we discover new failure modes. Without that feedback loop, it’s very easy to confuse more activity with better intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response says accurate testing grounds the research cycle and that reliable tests guide research effort, but does not state that testing makes evaluation of each research attempt reliable.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention subagents testing different research ideas in parallel.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that subagents cross-validate research results.
